question: Which statement best describes The document frame?
options: `<h2>` introduces a major section under the page’s main heading. It is like a chapter title under the book title. Use it when the content begins a new major part, not merely to make text large. A screen reader can use headings to jump through a page. In practice, a screen reader can list the page headings so someone can jump to a section. In practice, a paragraph can contain inline links or emphasis while preserving one text idea.

`<h3>` introduces a subsection within a larger section. It is like a section label inside a chapter. Do not skip levels only to get a smaller visual size; choose the level that matches the content outline. Then style the heading with CSS if its appearance needs adjustment. In practice, a heading’s visual size belongs in CSS; its level belongs to the outline. In practice, use CSS margins to set paragraph spacing instead of empty paragraphs.

`

` marks a paragraph of related sentences. It gives the browser a meaningful text block and creates default spacing. It is like grouping sentences on one note card. Use paragraphs for prose rather than adding line breaks after every sentence, which makes the document harder to edit and understand. In practice, split a long explanation into paragraphs when the subject or point changes. In practice, a visual design can restyle h2 and h3 while keeping their hierarchy intact.

`<h1>` is usually the main heading that describes the page. It helps readers understand what the page is about. It is like the title on a book cover. A page can have more than one heading in some structures, but keep the outline clear and make the main subject easy to find. In practice, a recipe page can use one main heading, then headings for ingredients and steps. In practice, write a heading that names the section rather than repeating a generic label.
